tagline: A pastoral letter of hard-edged wisdom from James, the brother of Jesus, insisting that real faith shows itself in endurance, speech, mercy, and deeds.
overview:
James reads less like an argument and more like a collection of sharp, practical sayings strung together by a pastor who has watched faith go soft. It addresses believers under pressure: tested by hardship, tempted to flatter the rich and ignore the poor, quarrelsome, loose with their tongues, and confident about tomorrow's business plans. James moves quickly from one subject to the next, but a few convictions hold it together. God gives wisdom generously to anyone who asks. Trials can make a person whole rather than bitter. And faith that never becomes action is not faith at all.

The letter is short (five chapters, 108 verses) and full of pictures: a wave tossed by the wind, a man who looks in a mirror and forgets his face, a spark that sets a forest ablaze, a mist that vanishes, a farmer waiting for rain. It echoes the wisdom books of the Old Testament, especially Proverbs, and it echoes the teaching of Jesus even more, above all the Sermon on the Mount, though it rarely quotes him directly.

James matters because it guards a door the church keeps leaving open: the idea that believing the right things is enough. Its most famous line, that a person is justified by deeds and not by faith alone (2:24), has troubled readers who love Paul's letters, and the question of how the two fit is one of the great conversations in Christian theology. Read carefully, James does not offer a different gospel. It describes what the gospel produces in a life, and it refuses to let the poor be forgotten while the church talks about faith.
author:
The letter names its author only as “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). The name is the Greek form of Jacob, and several men in the New Testament bear it. James the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve, was executed by Herod Agrippa I around AD 44 (Acts 12:2), probably too early to have written it. The church's tradition has long identified the author as James the brother of Jesus (Mark 6:3; Galatians 1:19), who did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5), saw the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:7), and became the leading figure in the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13-21; 21:18; Galatians 2:9). The Jewish historian Josephus reports that this James was stoned at the instigation of the high priest Ananus around AD 62. Christians have understood his relation to Jesus in three ways: a younger son of Joseph and Mary (the common Protestant view), a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage (the Eastern Orthodox view), or a cousin (the traditional Roman Catholic view, going back to Jerome).

The case for James the Lord's brother rests on the unadorned self-description (only someone well known could sign simply as James), the letter's deeply Jewish character, its closeness to the teaching of Jesus, and its fit with the James of Acts 15, whose speech shares some vocabulary with the letter. Many modern scholars instead regard the letter as pseudonymous, written later in James's name, pointing to its polished Greek, its slow acceptance into the canon (the fourth-century historian Eusebius listed it among the disputed books), and what they read as a response to a later form of Pauline teaching. A mediating view holds that the letter preserves James's teaching, gathered and put into literary Greek by a disciple, perhaps after his death. Defenders of authorship by James reply that Galilee was bilingual, that a Jerusalem leader could have used a capable scribe, and that late recognition may reflect the letter's limited circulation among Jewish believers rather than doubts about its origin.
date: If James the brother of Jesus wrote it, the letter comes before his death around AD 62. Within that window some place it very early, in the mid-40s, which would make it among the first New Testament writings: it says nothing about the controversy over circumcising Gentile converts settled at the Jerusalem council around AD 49 (Acts 15), it calls the gathering a synagogue (2:2), and its church organization is simple. Others place it in the late 50s or early 60s, reading chapter 2 as a response to people who had heard Paul's teaching on faith and bent it into an excuse for inaction. Scholars who regard the letter as pseudonymous usually date it between about AD 70 and 100, and a few later still. The earliest clear quotations of James by name come from Origen in the third century, which is part of what keeps the question open.
setting:
The letter is addressed “To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion” (1:1). The Dispersion (in Greek, diaspora) was the standard term for Jews living outside the land of Israel, scattered across the Roman and Parthian worlds since the Assyrian and Babylonian exiles. Whether James means Jewish believers in Jesus living abroad, or the whole church pictured as God's renewed Israel in exile, is debated; either way the readers are steeped in the Scriptures and customs of Israel. They know the law, Abraham, Rahab, Job, and Elijah without explanation.

The world behind the letter is agrarian and sharply divided by wealth. Rich landowners hold back wages from day laborers who mow their fields (5:4), drag poorer people into court (2:6), and arrive at the assembly in gold rings and fine clothes (2:2). Merchants plan trading trips from city to city (4:13). Farmers wait on the fall and spring rains (5:7), a detail that fits the climate of Palestine and Syria, where autumn rains soften the ground for planting and spring rains fill out the grain. Behind it all lies the pressure on Jerusalem and Judea in the decades before the revolt against Rome in AD 66, a period marked by economic strain, factional violence, and resentment of the wealthy priestly families.
purpose: James writes to form a community whose faith is whole, not divided. He calls the double-minded person (1:8; 4:8) the chief danger: someone who prays but doubts, who hears but does not do, who blesses God and curses people with the same tongue, who wants friendship with God and with the world at once. Against that division James sets the single-hearted life: endurance under trial, prayer for wisdom, care for orphans and widows, impartial love for the poor, controlled speech, humility before God, patience until the Lord comes, and prayer for the sick and the wandering. The letter is pastoral correction for a church that has let status, anger, and talk crowd out obedience, and it speaks to believers who are suffering at the hands of the powerful as well as to believers tempted to imitate them.
story: James belongs to the story after Pentecost, when the good news about Jesus had spread from Jerusalem into the wider world and communities of believers were learning to live it out under pressure. It stands first among the letters traditionally called the General or Catholic Letters (James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1 to 3 John, and Jude), addressed to the church broadly rather than to one city. Its roots run deep into the Old Testament: the law given at Sinai, the wisdom of Proverbs, and the prophets' anger at the oppression of the poor (compare 5:1-6 with Amos). It stands beside the Gospels as a witness to how Jesus' own teaching was lived in the earliest Jewish-Christian communities, and alongside Paul it shows the church holding together grace received and obedience lived.
christ: James names Jesus only twice (1:1; 2:1), and some readers have concluded that the letter says little about him. That misses how much of James is Jesus' own teaching. The call to rejoice in trials, to ask God who gives generously, to be doers and not only hearers, to show mercy, to refuse oaths (5:12, closely echoing Matthew 5:33-37), to honor the poor who are heirs of the kingdom, and to warn the rich whose treasures rot all sound the notes of the Sermon on the Mount and the Sermon on the Plain. James calls Jesus “our glorious Lord Jesus Christ” (2:1), looks for “the Lord’s coming” (5:7-8), and presents him as the Judge who “is standing at the door” (5:9). The brother who once did not believe now calls himself Jesus' servant. The letter shows Christ as Lord of the whole of life, whose word is planted in believers (1:21) and bears fruit in mercy.
reading:
Read James as wisdom literature in the form of a letter, closer to Proverbs or to Jesus' sermons than to Romans. It gathers short units of teaching on recurring subjects (trials, wisdom, wealth, speech, faith and deeds) and returns to them from different angles, often linking sections by a repeated word. Don't look for a single tidy outline; watch instead for the threads that run through the whole. James uses vivid, even blunt language (“You adulteresses” in 4:4 draws on the prophets' picture of Israel's unfaithfulness to God) and expects readers to feel its force.

The most common misreading is to set James against Paul as if one taught salvation by faith and the other salvation by effort. Both teach that God saves by grace, and both insist that true faith is living and active. They use the words faith, works, and justify in different senses and against different errors. Another misreading treats the letter as a list of moral tips. James is theological throughout: it grounds its commands in who God is, the unchanging Father who gives every good gift and chose to give his people new birth through the word of truth.

structure.title: Trials, wisdom, and the word
structure.summary: James opens with the main themes of the letter: joy and endurance in trials, wisdom asked for in faith, the reversal of rich and poor, the source of temptation, and the call to be doers of the word rather than hearers only.

structure.title: Faith that shows no favoritism and faith that works
structure.summary: Favoring the rich breaks the royal law of love. Faith without deeds is dead, as Abraham and Rahab show.

structure.title: The tongue and the wisdom from above
structure.summary: Teachers face stricter judgment, the tongue is a small fire that can burn a whole life, and true wisdom is known by its peaceable, merciful fruit.

structure.title: Pride, worldliness, and wealth
structure.summary: Quarrels spring from disordered desires. James calls the double-minded to humble themselves before God, rebukes slander and arrogant planning, and pronounces judgment on rich oppressors.

structure.title: Patience, prayer, and restoring the wanderer
structure.summary: Believers wait patiently for the Lord's coming, keep plain speech, pray in every circumstance including sickness, and bring back those who stray.

themes.title: Trials and endurance
themes.body: James opens by telling believers to consider trials an occasion for joy, not because suffering is good in itself but because tested faith produces perseverance, and perseverance leads to maturity. The theme returns at the end with the prophets and Job as examples of patience. James is honest that trials hurt and that people under pressure are tempted to blame God; he insists that God tempts no one and gives only good gifts.

themes.title: Faith and deeds
themes.body: The heart of James 2 is that faith which does nothing is dead. James is not dismissing faith; he writes to people who say they have it. His target is a faith of words and bare agreement, the kind that tells a hungry person to stay warm and well fed and does nothing. Abraham's offering of Isaac and Rahab's welcome of the spies show what living faith looks like when it is tested. Readers have reconciled this with Paul in several ways: the two use justify differently (Paul for God's verdict on the sinner, James for the showing of that verdict in a life), they mean different things by faith and by works, or James corrects a distorted slogan drawn from Paul's teaching. Roman Catholic teaching adds that justification grows through good works done by grace. Chapter 2's note sets these out.

themes.title: The poor and the rich
themes.body: Few books of the Bible speak as sharply about wealth. James tells the lowly believer to take pride in his high position, warns the rich that they will fade like a flower, condemns favoritism in the assembly, and pronounces woe on landowners who withhold wages. Standing in the line of the prophets and of Jesus, James declares that God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith.

themes.title: Speech
themes.body: Every chapter touches the tongue: quick to listen and slow to speak (1:19), empty words to the hungry (2:16), the tongue as a fire (3:6), slander and boasting (4:11-16), grumbling and oaths (5:9-12). For James, speech is the clearest test of whether faith has reached the whole person.

themes.title: Wisdom from above
themes.body: Wisdom in James is not cleverness but a way of life that comes as God's gift. It is asked for in prayer (1:5) and known by its fruit: purity, peace, gentleness, mercy, and sincerity (3:17). James contrasts it with an earthly wisdom marked by jealousy and selfish ambition, which produces disorder.

keyChapters.why: It sets out the letter's themes, from trials and wisdom to the call to be doers of the word and the definition of pure religion.
The famous discussion of faith and deeds, and the sharpest New Testament rebuke of favoritism toward the rich.
The Bible's fullest reflection on the power of speech, and the contrast between earthly wisdom and the wisdom from above.
Judgment on oppressive wealth, patience until the Lord's coming, and the practice of prayer and anointing for the sick.

parts.body:
James is a short letter, five chapters and 108 verses, and it reads in about fifteen minutes. It is not built like a long argument. It reads more like a string of sharp, practical sayings from a pastor who has watched faith go soft. It moves quickly from one subject to the next and keeps coming back to the same few: hard times, wisdom, money, speech, and what real faith does.

Its first readers were believers under pressure. Many were poor. Some were being cheated of their wages and dragged into court by rich men (2:6; 5:4). And inside the church things had gone wrong too. Rich visitors were given the best seats while the poor were told to stand (2:2-3). People quarrelled, cursed one another, and made big business plans without a thought for God (4:1-2, 13).

James answers with pictures that stay in the mind: a wave tossed by the wind, a man who looks in a mirror and forgets his own face, a small spark that sets a whole forest on fire, a mist that is gone by noon, a farmer waiting for the rain. His one great conviction runs through all of them. Faith that never becomes action is not living faith. “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only” (1:22).

The letter has a famous hard verse: “a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone” (2:24). Readers who love Paul's letters have asked for centuries how this fits with Paul. These notes set out how the churches answer, fairly, and they say first what all of them confess: God saves by grace, and the faith that saves is never dead.

James is also tender. It says God gives wisdom “generously to all without finding fault” (1:5). It says that God tempts no one and that “Every good and perfect gift is from above” (1:17). And it ends not with a farewell but with a church gathered round the sick, praying, confessing and bringing back the one who has wandered.

The letter begins, “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). James is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Jacob, and several men in the New Testament bear it. James the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve, was put to death by Herod Agrippa I around AD 44 (Acts 12:2), which is most likely too early for him to have written it.

From early times the church has held that the writer was James the brother of Jesus. Mark names him first among Jesus' brothers (Mark 6:3). During Jesus' ministry he did not believe: “For even His own brothers did not believe in Him” (John 7:5). After the resurrection Jesus appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), and he became a leader of the church in Jerusalem. Paul calls him “James, the Lord’s brother” (Galatians 1:19) and names him among the ‘pillars’ there (Galatians 2:9), and he speaks for the church at the council in Acts 15. The Jewish historian Josephus reports that this James was stoned at the instigation of the high priest Ananus around AD 62.

Christians have understood his relation to Jesus in three ways. Many Protestants hold that he was a younger son of Joseph and Mary. The Orthodox churches hold that he was a son of Joseph by an earlier marriage. Traditional Catholic teaching, going back to Jerome, holds that he was a cousin. The notes on Mark 3:31-35 set these out.

Why do many think this James wrote the letter? He signs with his first name alone, which only a well-known leader could do. The letter is deeply Jewish. It is full of echoes of Jesus' own teaching. And it fits the James of Acts 15: the letter sent from that council opens with the same one-word greeting, ‘Greetings’ (Acts 15:23), that James 1:1 uses.

Many modern scholars hold instead that someone wrote the letter later in James's name. They point to its polished Greek; to how slowly the whole church came to use it; and to chapter 2, which they read as an answer to a later, twisted form of Paul's teaching. Others take a middle view: the teaching is James's own, gathered and put into good Greek by a disciple, perhaps after his death. Those who hold that James himself wrote it reply that Galilee was a place where people spoke Greek as well as Aramaic, that a leader in Jerusalem could have used a skilled helper, and that a letter sent to Jewish believers might simply have travelled less widely at first.

These notes do not choose. They call the writer ‘James’, as the letter does. The church came to receive the letter as Scripture everywhere, though it took time. In the 300s the historian Eusebius listed it among the books some still disputed. By 367 Athanasius of Alexandria counted it in the New Testament, and the North African councils of the late 300s did the same.

parts.h: Who it was written to, and when
parts.body:
The letter is addressed “To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion” (1:1). ‘The Dispersion’ (in Greek, diaspora) was the usual name for the Jews who lived outside the land of Israel, scattered across the world since the exiles to Assyria and Babylon. Some readers think James means Jewish believers in Jesus living abroad. Others think he speaks of the whole church as God's people in exile, far from home. Either way, the readers knew Israel's Scriptures well. James can name Abraham, Rahab, Job and Elijah without explaining who they were.

The world behind the letter is a world of farms and of a deep gap between rich and poor. Rich landowners hold back the pay of the day labourers who mow their fields (5:4). Merchants plan trading trips from city to city (4:13). Farmers wait on the fall and spring rains (5:7), which fits the weather of Palestine and Syria. The meeting place is called by the word for a synagogue (2:2, ‘meeting’ in the BSB).

When was it written? If James the brother of Jesus wrote it, it comes before his death around AD 62. Some place it very early, in the mid-40s, which would make it one of the first books of the New Testament. They note that it says nothing of the argument over circumcising Gentile believers that the council in Jerusalem settled around AD 49, and that the church it pictures is simple. Others place it in the late 50s or early 60s, and read chapter 2 as an answer to people who had bent Paul's teaching on faith into an excuse to do nothing. Scholars who think it was written later in James's name usually date it between about AD 70 and 100.

The earliest writer known to quote James by name is Origen, in the 200s, which is part of why the question stays open. These notes do not choose.

James does not follow one tidy outline. Like the book of Proverbs, it gathers short units of teaching and returns to its subjects from different sides. It often links one saying to the next by a repeated word: ‘Greetings’ (chairein) in 1:1 leads to ‘joy’ (chara) in 1:2; ‘not lacking anything’ in 1:4 leads to ‘if any of you lacks wisdom’ in 1:5.

Trials, wisdom and the word (chapter 1). Joy in hard times; asking God for wisdom; the poor raised up and the rich brought low; where temptation comes from; the good gifts of the Father; hearing and doing. The last two verses set the agenda for the rest: a bridled tongue, care for orphans and widows, and a life kept clean from the world's ways.

Faith that shows no favouritism, and faith that works (chapter 2). Honouring the rich and shaming the poor breaks the ‘royal law’ of love. Faith without deeds is dead, as Abraham and Rahab show.

The tongue and the wisdom from above (chapter 3). Teachers face a stricter judgment. The tongue is small and can burn a whole life. True wisdom is known by its peace and mercy.

Pride, the world and wealth (4:1 to 5:6). Quarrels come from desires at war inside us. James calls the divided heart to humble itself before God. He forbids slander and boasting about tomorrow, and he speaks like a prophet against rich men who cheat their workers.

Patience, prayer and bringing people back (5:7-20). Wait for the Lord's coming like a farmer waits for rain. Keep plain speech. Pray in every situation, including sickness. Bring back the one who wanders.

parts.h: Faith and works: James and Paul
parts.body:
This is the passage most readers have heard about. James writes to people who say they have faith but do nothing with it. He pictures a brother or sister without clothes or food, and a believer who says, “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed,” but does not help (2:16). “So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead” (2:17). Then he names Abraham, who offered Isaac, and Rahab, who hid Israel's spies, and he concludes, “As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone” (2:24).

Paul writes, “For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:28). Both writers quote the same verse about Abraham: “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). So how can both be true?

Start with what all the churches confess. Salvation is God's gift, by his grace. No one earns it, and no one can boast. And the faith that saves is never a dead faith that does nothing. Paul says so himself: “All that matters is faith, expressed through love” (Galatians 5:6). In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint statement that ‘by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit on our part, we are accepted by God’, while naming differences that remain.

Most readers, across the churches, think James and Paul are answering different questions, and they point to three words. ‘Justify’: Paul uses it most often for God's verdict on a sinner; James may use it for showing that someone is truly righteous, as when Jesus says, “wisdom is vindicated by all her children” (Luke 7:35). Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, and his faith was shown and completed decades later in Genesis 22. ‘Faith’: Paul means trust in Christ; James attacks a bare agreement with the right words, the kind even demons have (2:19). ‘Works’: Paul rejects works of the law as the ground of God's acceptance; James asks for deeds of mercy as the fruit of faith. Some add that James may be answering people who had turned Paul's teaching into a slogan, so that the two men face one error from opposite sides.

Yet the churches still put James 2:24 in different words. Protestant churches teach that a person is justified by faith alone, as a verdict God gives once, and that good works always follow as the fruit and the evidence of a living faith, never as its ground. Many of them read 2:24 as faith shown to be real. The Westminster Confession of 1646 puts it this way: faith is the only instrument of justification, yet it is never alone in the justified person. The Catholic Church teaches that grace comes first and can never be earned, and that by grace a person is not only forgiven but truly made righteous. At the Council of Trent in 1547 it read 2:24 as speaking of growth in justification through good works done by God's grace. The Orthodox churches speak of salvation as union with God and a sharing in his life by grace, and of justification as one true picture among many, not separated from the healing of the whole person. For them justification never became the dividing question it became in the West.

Martin Luther, in the prefaces to his New Testament of 1522, ranked James below the letters he thought showed Christ most clearly, and famously called it ‘an epistle of straw’ by comparison. These notes do not choose between the churches. The doctrine study ‘Justification’ sets out each view at length.

Whatever words a church uses, James will not let any of us rest in a faith of talk. The test he gives is very plain: a hungry person in front of you.

Few books of the Bible speak as sharply about money as James. The poor believer should take pride in his ‘high position’, and the rich one in his ‘low position’, for the rich “will pass away like a flower of the field” (1:10). God has “chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith” (2:5). And in chapter 5 James speaks over rich landowners as the prophets did: “Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you” (5:4).

He stands in a long line. The law of Moses said, “You are to pay his wages each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them” (Deuteronomy 24:15). Amos spoke against those “who trample the needy” (Amos 8:4). Jesus said, “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke 6:20), and “But woe to you who are rich” (Luke 6:24).

James is not writing a plan for a political party, and his words do not belong to one side. He does not say that every rich person is wicked or that every poor person is good. He names particular wrongs: unpaid wages, unfair courts, luxury built on other people's want, and a church that copies the world by giving the best seat to the best-dressed. The sharpest edge of chapter 2 is turned on the church itself.

That edge reaches every reader. Most of us have looked twice at someone who seemed important and past someone who did not. James calls it what it is: favouritism, and a sin against the royal law, “Love your neighbor as yourself” (2:8).

parts.h: The tongue, and the wisdom from above
parts.body:
Every chapter of James touches speech. Be “quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (1:19). Do not offer warm words to the hungry instead of food (2:16). Do not slander or grumble (4:11; 5:9). And let your yes mean yes (5:12).

Chapter 3 gathers it all. The tongue is small, like a horse's bit or a ship's rudder, yet it steers a whole life. It is a spark that sets a forest on fire. And it is double: “With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness” (3:9). To curse a person is to dishonour the God whose likeness that person bears.

James includes himself: “We all stumble in many ways” (3:2). He does not pretend that anyone has mastered the tongue.

Then he turns to wisdom. There is a wisdom that is clever and proud, full of ‘bitter jealousy and selfish ambition’, and it brings disorder (3:14-16). And there is the wisdom God gives: “first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere” (3:17). That wisdom is not a gift for the clever. It is promised to anyone who asks God for it (1:5).

parts.h: Trials, temptation, and the good Father
parts.body:
James begins with a hard word: “Consider it pure joy, my brothers, when you encounter trials of many kinds” (1:2). He does not say trials are pleasant, or that pain is good in itself, or that a suffering person should pretend to be happy. He says that faith which is tested learns to endure, and that endurance makes a person mature and complete (1:3-4).

He is honest that hardship can turn into temptation. The same Greek word can mean a trial from outside or a temptation to sin from within. And when people suffer, they are tempted to blame God. James will not allow it: “When tempted, no one should say, ‘God is tempting me.’ For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone” (1:13). Sin grows from our own desires. What comes from God is only good: “Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow” (1:17).

Nothing in James says that a person's suffering is God punishing them. The letter points instead to Job, who suffered without being to blame, and to the God who is “full of compassion and mercy” (5:11). If you are carrying something heavy now, James does not ask you to feel joy on demand. He tells the suffering to pray, and the church to pray with them (5:13-14). Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Near the end James writes, “Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven” (5:14-15).

The elders were the leaders of the congregation. Olive oil was used in James's day as a medicine, and also to mark a person as set apart for God. Jesus' disciples “healed many of the sick, anointing them with oil” (Mark 6:13).

Christians read the promise in more than one way. Many take it as a real promise of God's help, which often comes as healing in this life and comes fully in the resurrection; the Greek words for ‘restore’ and ‘raise up’ can carry both meanings. Others stress that healing depends on God's will, as Paul's thorn shows (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). The Catholic and Orthodox churches see in these verses the ground of a sacrament, the anointing of the sick. Many Protestant churches see the oil as medicine, a sign, or both, and some anoint the sick with prayer as James describes. None of these readings sets prayer against a doctor. Oil was itself a medicine.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

parts.h: James and the teaching of Jesus
parts.body:
James names Jesus only twice (1:1; 2:1). Some readers have concluded that the letter says little about him. That misses how much of James is Jesus' own teaching, heard and lived. James rarely quotes his brother word for word, but the echoes are everywhere.

Jesus said, “Ask, and it will be given to you” (Matthew 7:7); James says ask God for wisdom and “it will be given to him” (1:5). Jesus told of the man who “hears these words of Mine and does not act on them” (Matthew 7:26); James warns against being a hearer only. Jesus blessed the merciful and the peacemakers (Matthew 5:7, 9), and blessed the poor and warned the rich (Luke 6:20, 24); so does James. Jesus warned against treasure that ‘moth and rust destroy’ (Matthew 6:19); James says, “Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes” (5:2). Jesus said, “Do not judge” (Matthew 7:1); James asks, “But who are you to judge your neighbor?” (4:12). And James's word on oaths, “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be yes, and your ‘No,’ no” (5:12), is nearly the same as Jesus' own (Matthew 5:37).

James calls Jesus “our glorious Lord Jesus Christ” (2:1), and waits for “the Lord’s coming” (5:7). This is a striking thing for a brother to write. The man who once did not believe now calls himself Jesus' servant.

James is soaked in Israel's Scriptures. It is closest to the wisdom books, above all Proverbs, with their short sayings about the tongue, pride, and the shortness of life. It quotes Proverbs 3:34 directly: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (4:6). It cites the law: “Love your neighbor as yourself” (2:8, from Leviticus 19:18), and two of the Ten Commandments (2:11). It echoes the Shema, Israel's daily confession that God is one (2:19; Deuteronomy 6:4).

It speaks like the prophets against those who cheat the poor, and calls an unfaithful people ‘adulteresses’ (4:4), the prophets' picture of Israel as a wife who has left her husband. It names Abraham, Rahab, Job and Elijah as examples, and assumes its readers know their stories.

Sometimes the wording in James differs from the Old Testament passage in your Bible. Proverbs 3:34 in the BSB reads, “He mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble”, while James has “God opposes the proud”. New Testament writers often quoted the old Greek translation of the Old Testament, as the notes on Hebrews explain, and the chapter notes point out such differences.

It is not a different gospel from Paul's. Both teach that God saves by grace, and both teach that living faith acts. They use some of the same words in different senses and against different errors.

It is not a list of moral tips. James grounds every command in who God is: the generous giver, the unchanging Father, the one Lawgiver and Judge, the Lord who is full of compassion and mercy.

It is not a promise that strong faith brings health and wealth. James says the poor are rich in faith, and he points to Job and the prophets, who suffered. Teaching that faith guarantees health and riches is an error.

It is not a teaching that sickness comes from weak faith or hidden sin. James says only “If he has sinned”, not that sickness always comes from sin.

It is not a weapon for one political side against another. It speaks to the rich who cheat and to the church that flatters them, and its sharpest words are turned on the believers themselves.

And it is not a cold book. It begins with joy and ends with a church that goes out after the one who has wandered.

Read it in one sitting, and read it aloud. It takes about fifteen minutes.

Read it as wisdom, closer to Proverbs and the Sermon on the Mount than to Romans. Do not look for one tidy outline. Watch instead for the threads that run through the whole: trials, wisdom, rich and poor, the tongue, faith and deeds. Notice the words that return: ‘perfect’ or ‘complete’, ‘double-minded’, ‘doer’, ‘mercy’, ‘humble’.

Read chapter 2 slowly, and read it beside Romans 4 and Galatians 2, and then read Ephesians 2:8-10, where Paul holds both together: saved by grace through faith, “created in Christ Jesus to do good works”.

Where churches differ, on faith and works, on the anointing of the sick, on who wrote the letter, read more than one view before you settle, and hold your own view as one who may yet be taught.

And let it ask its plain questions. What have you done with what you have heard? How do you treat the person who cannot repay you? What did your tongue do today? And whom do you know who has wandered?

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: ‘Consider it pure joy’ in trials: not pretending, and not calling pain good.
‘God is tempting me.’ Testing and temptation, and why God is never the source of sin.
‘Pure and undefiled religion’: orphans and widows, and a bridled tongue.
Favouritism in the meeting, and God's choice of the poor.
‘Guilty of breaking all of it’, and ‘Mercy triumphs over judgment’.
‘Not by faith alone.’ James and Paul, and how the churches read 2:24.
‘We who teach will be judged more strictly.’
The tongue ‘set on fire by hell’: Gehenna and what it means.
‘You adulteresses’, friendship with the world, and the hard verse 4:5.
‘If the Lord is willing.’ Plans, and the shortness of life.
Woe to the rich who withheld wages: a prophet's word, not a party's.
Anointing the sick and ‘the prayer of faith’. Never a verdict that the sick lack faith.
Turning back the one who wanders, and covering ‘a multitude of sins’.

words.line: Greek diaspora, the scattering: Jews living outside the land of Israel, or the church pictured as God's people far from home (1:1).
Greek peirasmos, a test from outside or a pull to sin from within. The same hardship can lead either way (1:2, 12-14).
Greek dipsuchos, literally ‘two-souled’: a heart divided between God and something else (1:8; 4:8).
Greek poiētēs, one who does or makes. ‘Be doers of the word’ is the heart of chapter 1 (1:22-25).
Greek thrēskeia, the outward practice of worship. James says what God counts as pure religion (1:26-27).
Greek prosōpolēmpsia, literally ‘receiving the face’: judging people by how they look (2:1, 9).
Greek erga, things done. For James, deeds of faith and mercy, like feeding the hungry (2:14-26).
Greek dikaioō, to declare righteous or to show to be righteous. Readers differ on which James means (2:21-25).
The word behind ‘hell’ in 3:6, from the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a name for the place of final judgment.
Greek philia, friendship that shares loyalties and enemies. Its only use in the New Testament (4:4).
Greek makrothumia, being ‘long-tempered’: bearing people and hardship without giving up or hitting back (5:7-10).
Greek presbuteroi, the recognised leaders of the congregation, called to pray over the sick (5:14).

timeline.what: God counts Abram's faith as righteousness (Genesis 15:6); years later Abraham offers Isaac (Genesis 22). James joins the two (2:21-23).
Rahab hides Israel's spies at Jericho and is spared (Joshua 2; 6:25). James names her beside Abraham (2:25).
Elijah prays, and there is no rain, and then rain again (1 Kings 17 to 18; James 5:17-18).
His brothers do not believe in him (John 7:5).
The risen Jesus appears to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), who becomes a leader of the church in Jerusalem.
Herod Agrippa I puts James the son of Zebedee to death (Acts 12:2).
The reign of Claudius, when a famine strikes Judea and the church at Antioch sends help (Acts 11:28-30).
The council in Jerusalem; James speaks for the church (Acts 15:13-21).
The letter is written, if James the brother of Jesus wrote it. Some place it early, others in the late 50s or early 60s.
Josephus reports that the high priest Ananus had James the brother of Jesus stoned.
The Jewish revolt against Rome begins.
The date most often given by scholars who think the letter was written later in James's name.
Origen is the earliest writer known to quote James by name.
Athanasius of Alexandria lists James among the books of the New Testament.
Luther's preface ranks James below the letters he thought showed Christ most clearly.

map.title: The one place on this map

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: The letter names no place. The church has long named James the brother of Jesus as the writer, and he led the church here (Acts 15:13; Galatians 2:9). If he wrote it, he most likely wrote from here.

teaching.mapNote: | James names no place on earth. It is written to ‘the twelve tribes of the Dispersion’, scattered abroad. The map shows only Jerusalem, where the James the church has long named as the writer led the church. The letter itself does not say where it was written.
